items: Find 2/3 of 30 laddoos
How many 1/2 L bottles can be filled from 6 L?
Cost of 3/4 kg at ₹80 per kg
Share 3/4 of a pizza equally among 3 friends
Area of a card 1/2 m by 1/3 m
How many 1/4-hour slots are in 2 hours?

quiz.q: A recipe for 4 people needs 3/4 cup of sugar. How much sugar is needed for 6 people?
quiz.explain: For 1 person: 3/4 ÷ 4 = 3/16 cup. For 6 people: 3/16 × 6 = 18/16 = 1 1/8 cups.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 3/4 by 6 without first finding the amount for one person

quiz.q: A train goes 60 km in one hour. How far does it go in 2 1/2 hours at the same speed?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the half hour or divides instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Aisha reads 2/5 of a 150-page book on Sunday. How many pages are left to read?
quiz.explain: She read 2/5 × 150 = 60 pages. Pages left = 150 − 60 = 90.
quiz.mistake: Gives the pages she read instead of the pages left

quiz.q: Harpreet pours a 2 L jug of lassi into glasses that hold 1/5 L each. How many glasses does she fill?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 2 by 1/5 instead of dividing

quiz.q: Joseph has a 5 m rope. He uses 1/2 of it, and then 1/3 of what is left. How much rope remains?
quiz.explain: After using half, 5/2 m is left. 1/3 of 5/2 is 5/6. Remaining: 5/2 − 5/6 = 15/6 − 5/6 = 10/6 = 1 2/3 m.
quiz.mistake: Takes 1/3 of the whole rope instead of 1/3 of what is left

quiz.q: A family eats 3/4 kg of rice every day. How much rice do they eat in a week?
quiz.mistake: Adds 7 and 3/4 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: ₹240 is shared. Riya gets 1/3 of it and Joseph gets 1/4 of it. How much money is left?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts only one person's share

items: Riya
Joseph
Left

quiz.q: Kabir multiplied 12 by 2/3 and got 18. Is his answer reasonable?
options: Yes — multiplying always makes a number bigger
No — multiplying by a fraction less than 1 should give less than 12
quiz.explain: 2/3 is less than 1, so 2/3 of 12 must be less than 12. The correct answer is 8.
quiz.mistake: Thinks multiplying always increases a number

teach.ask: Gappu is solving fraction stories. How does he know when to multiply and when to divide?
teach.praise: Brilliant! 'Of' means multiply, 'how many fit' means divide. Gappu is a fraction detective!
teach.nudge: Which word in a story tells you to multiply?

learn.hook: Two ₹10 coins of the same kind are perfect twins — put one on the other and they match exactly!
points: Two figures are congruent if they have the same shape AND the same size.
To test, imagine placing one figure exactly on top of the other (superimposing). If they cover each other fully, they are congruent.
We use the symbol ≅ for 'is congruent to'.
Line segments are congruent if they have the same length. Angles are congruent if they have the same measure. Circles are congruent if they have the same radius.
A figure and its mirror image (flipped) are also congruent.

example.q: Which pairs are congruent: (a) two pages of the same notebook, (b) a photo and its enlarged print, (c) two circles of radius 3 cm?
steps: (a) Same shape and size — they match exactly
(b) Same shape but different size — not congruent
(c) Same radius, so the circles match exactly

learn.reallife: Factories make thousands of congruent things — bottle caps, bricks, coins and tiles — so that they all fit the same way.

games.title: Twins or not?
items: Two ₹10 coins of the same kind
Two pages of the same notebook
A photo and its enlarged print
Two circles of radius 3 cm
Squares of side 4 cm and 5 cm
Two 40° angles
A 4 cm line and a 6 cm line
A flag sticker and a big flag

games.title: Congruence check
items: Congruent figures have the same shape and the same size.
Both shape and size must match.
All squares are congruent.
Squares always have the same shape, but their sizes can differ.
Two circles with the same radius are congruent.
The radius decides the size of a circle.
A figure and its mirror image are congruent.
Flip one over and it fits exactly on the other.
Two triangles with the same area must be congruent.
A 6 cm base with 2 cm height and a 4 cm base with 3 cm height both give area 6 cm², but the triangles differ.
Two line segments of the same length are congruent.
Same length means one fits exactly on the other.

quiz.q: What does it mean when two figures are congruent?
quiz.explain: Congruent figures match exactly when placed one on top of the other, so both shape and size are the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the same shape is enough

quiz.q: Line segment AB is 5 cm and PQ is 5 cm. Are they congruent?
options: Yes, because they have the same length
No, because they have different names
Only if they point the same way
quiz.explain: Line segments with equal lengths are congruent; their names and directions do not matter.
quiz.mistake: Thinks position or labels decide congruence

quiz.q: Which pair is ALWAYS congruent?
quiz.explain: Circles with the same radius are always the same size and shape.
quiz.mistake: Thinks figures of the same type are always congruent

quiz.q: ∠B is congruent to ∠A, and ∠A = 70°. What is ∠B?
quiz.explain: Congruent angles have the same measure, so ∠B = 70°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks congruent angles add up to 180°

quiz.q: Square ABCD ≅ square PQRS, and AB = 6 cm. What is the perimeter of PQRS?
quiz.explain: Congruent squares have equal sides, so PQ = 6 cm. Perimeter = 4 × 6 = 24 cm.
quiz.mistake: Gives the area (36) instead of the perimeter

quiz.q: What does the symbol ≅ mean?
quiz.explain: ≅ is read as 'is congruent to'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up geometry symbols

quiz.q: One rectangle is 4 cm by 3 cm and another is 6 cm by 2 cm. Both have area 12 cm². Are they congruent?
options: Only if they are the same colour
quiz.explain: One would not fit exactly on the other: the sides are 4 and 3 in one, and 6 and 2 in the other.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal area means congruent

quiz.q: How can you test whether two paper shapes are congruent?
options: Measure only one side of each
Place one exactly on top of the other and see if it covers it fully
quiz.explain: If one shape covers the other exactly (you may turn or flip it), the shapes are congruent.
quiz.mistake: Checks only one feature instead of the whole shape

teach.ask: Gappu found two leaves that look alike. When can he call two shapes 'congruent'? Explain!
teach.praise: Tweet! Same shape, same size, they fit exactly — Gappu found a pair of twin leaves!
teach.nudge: Is having the same shape enough? What else must be the same?

learn.hook: Do you have to check all six parts of two triangles to know they are twins? No! Just three are enough!
points: Two triangles are congruent if all three pairs of sides and all three pairs of angles match.
The order of letters matters: ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR means A matches P, B matches Q and C matches R.
SSS rule: if all three sides of one triangle equal the three sides of the other, the triangles are congruent.
SAS rule: if two sides and the angle BETWEEN them are equal, the triangles are congruent.
Two sides and an angle that is NOT between them is not always enough.

example.q: In ΔABC and ΔPQR, AB = PQ = 4 cm, BC = QR = 5 cm and CA = RP = 6 cm. Are they congruent?
steps: All three pairs of sides are equal
Matching vertices: A ↔ P, B ↔ Q, C ↔ R

learn.reallife: Bicycle frames and bridge supports use congruent triangles so that both sides carry the load equally.

items.text: SSS means three pairs of equal ___
In SAS, the angle must be ___ the two sides
If ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, then AC = ___
Two congruent triangles have ___ pairs of equal parts in all

quiz.q: ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR. Which side is equal to BC?
quiz.explain: B matches Q and C matches R, so BC matches QR.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the order of the letters

quiz.q: ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF and AB = 7 cm. What is DE?
quiz.explain: A matches D and B matches E, so DE = AB = 7 cm.
quiz.mistake: Does not use the matching order

quiz.q: One triangle has sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. Another has sides 5 cm, 3 cm and 4 cm. Are they congruent?
options: No, the sides are in a different order
Only if the angles are measured
quiz.explain: Both have the same three side lengths. Matching them up, all three pairs are equal, so they are congruent by SSS.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the order in which the sides are listed matters

quiz.q: Which information proves ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR by SAS?
quiz.explain: ∠B lies between sides AB and BC, and ∠Q lies between PQ and QR. That is Side–Angle–Side.
quiz.mistake: Uses an angle that is not between the two sides

quiz.q: ΔLMN ≅ ΔXYZ and ∠M = 65°. Which angle of ΔXYZ is 65°?
quiz.explain: M is the second letter, and so is Y. So ∠Y = ∠M = 65°.
quiz.mistake: Matches by position on the page instead of by letter order

quiz.q: ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR with AB = 4 cm, BC = 6 cm and CA = 5 cm. What is the perimeter of ΔPQR?
quiz.explain: Congruent triangles have equal sides, so the perimeter is the same: 4 + 6 + 5 = 15 cm.
quiz.mistake: Adds only two of the sides

quiz.q: In ΔABC, AB = AC and D is the midpoint of BC. Using only these facts, which rule shows ΔABD ≅ ΔACD?
quiz.explain: AB = AC (given), BD = CD (D is the midpoint) and AD is shared by both. Three pairs of sides are equal: SSS.
quiz.mistake: Picks a rule that needs an angle we were not given

quiz.q: Is 'three pairs of equal angles' (AAA) enough to say two triangles are congruent?
options: No — the triangles can be different sizes
quiz.explain: A small and a big equilateral triangle both have angles 60°, 60°, 60°, but they are not the same size.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal angles mean equal sides

teach.ask: Gappu has two triangles and wants to know if they are twins without checking all six parts. What shortcuts can he use?
teach.praise: Super! Three equal sides, or two sides with the angle between — Gappu loves these shortcuts!
teach.nudge: Which three parts are enough to check, and where must the angle be in SAS?

topics.title: More congruence rules: ASA, AAS and RHS

learn.hook: Two angles and one side can unlock a whole triangle — and right triangles have a special secret rule!
points: ASA rule: two angles and the side between them are equal → the triangles are congruent.
AAS: if two angles and a side NOT between them are equal, the third angles are equal too (angle sum 180°), so it becomes ASA.
RHS rule (only for right triangles): right angle, hypotenuse (longest side) and one more side equal → congruent.
AAA and SSA (angle not between the sides) are NOT congruence rules.
Once triangles are congruent, all their matching parts are equal. This helps us find unknown sides and angles.

example.q: In ΔABC and ΔPQR, ∠A = ∠P = 50°, AB = PQ = 6 cm and ∠B = ∠Q = 70°. Are they congruent? Find ∠R.
steps: Two angles and the side between them match, so the rule is ASA

learn.reallife: Carpenters check that two triangular shelf brackets are twins by matching one edge and the two angles at its ends.

games.title: Is it a congruence rule?
items: SSS
SAS
ASA
RHS
AAS
AAA
SSA (angle not between the sides)

items.q: Congruent right triangles: one hypotenuse is 13 cm. The other?
Congruent triangles: one has perimeter 18 cm. The other?

quiz.q: Two angles and the side between them in one triangle equal those in another. Which rule makes them congruent?
quiz.explain: Angle–Side–Angle: the side lies between the two angles.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the rule names

quiz.q: Two right triangles each have a hypotenuse of 10 cm and one other side of 6 cm. Which rule shows they are congruent?
quiz.explain: Right angle, Hypotenuse and one Side are equal: RHS.
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the right angle and the hypotenuse

quiz.q: In ΔABC and ΔPQR, ∠A = ∠P = 50°, ∠B = ∠Q = 70° and AB = PQ. What is ∠R?
quiz.explain: The triangles are congruent by ASA, so ∠R = ∠C = 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°.
quiz.mistake: Copies one of the given angles

quiz.q: Which set of equal parts is NOT enough to prove two triangles congruent?
options: Two sides and the angle between them
Two angles and the side between them
quiz.explain: Equal angles give the same shape, but the size can differ. AAA is not a congruence rule.
quiz.mistake: Thinks three equal parts of any kind are enough

quiz.q: ΔDEF ≅ ΔKLM by ASA, using ∠D = ∠K, DE = KL and ∠E = ∠L. Which side is equal to EF?
quiz.explain: E matches L and F matches M, so EF = LM.
quiz.mistake: Matches the sides in the wrong order

quiz.q: ∠A = ∠P = 40°, ∠B = ∠Q = 60° and BC = QR = 5 cm. Are ΔABC and ΔPQR congruent?
options: No, the side is not between the angles
Yes, by AAS (then ∠C = ∠R = 80°, so it becomes ASA)
quiz.explain: The third angles are both 180° − 40° − 60° = 80°. Now BC sits between ∠B and ∠C, so ASA applies.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the side must always be between the two given angles

quiz.q: Two ladders of the same length lean against a straight wall. Their feet are the same distance from the wall. Which rule shows the two triangles are congruent?
quiz.explain: The wall meets the ground at a right angle, the ladders are the equal hypotenuses, and the distances from the wall are equal sides: RHS. So both ladders reach the same height.
quiz.mistake: Does not spot the right angle at the wall

quiz.q: In kite ABCD, AB = AD and CB = CD. ∠ABC = 110°. What is ∠ADC?
quiz.explain: AB = AD, CB = CD and AC is shared, so ΔABC ≅ ΔADC by SSS. Matching angles are equal: ∠ADC = ∠ABC = 110°.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from 180° as if the angles were a linear pair

teach.ask: Gappu knows two angles and one side of a triangle. When are two such triangles congruent? Explain ASA to him!
teach.praise: Fantastic! Two angles with the side between them — ASA! Gappu is a congruence champion!
teach.nudge: Where must the side be, compared to the two angles?

learn.hook: Can two 'minuses' make a 'plus'? In integer multiplication — yes, they can! Let's see why.
points: Positive × positive = positive: 3 × 4 = 12.
Positive × negative = negative: 3 × (−4) means (−4) + (−4) + (−4) = −12.
Negative × positive = negative: (−4) × 3 = −12 (swapping the order does not change a product).
Negative × negative = positive: (−3) × (−4) = 12. The pattern 2 × (−4) = −8, 1 × (−4) = −4, 0 × (−4) = 0, (−1) × (−4) = 4 shows why.
With many factors: an even number of negative signs gives a positive answer, an odd number gives a negative answer.

example.q: Find (−4) × (−6), and check it with a pattern.

learn.reallife: Temperature falling by 3 degrees every hour, or losing 2 points for every wrong answer in a quiz, is multiplying with negative numbers.

quiz.q: What is (−7) × 6?
quiz.explain: A negative times a positive is negative. 7 × 6 = 42, so the answer is −42.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sign of the bigger number decides the answer

quiz.explain: Negative × negative = positive. 5 × 8 = 40, so the answer is 40.
quiz.mistake: Thinks two negatives give a negative

quiz.q: The temperature in Leh drops by 3 degrees every hour at night. What is the total change in degrees after 4 hours?
quiz.explain: A drop of 3 is −3. Four drops: 4 × (−3) = −12 degrees.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that a drop is a negative change

quiz.explain: 2 × 3 × 5 = 30. There are three negative signs (an odd number), so the answer is negative: −30.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any number of negatives makes a positive

quiz.q: Which product is positive?
quiz.explain: (−4) × (−5) × 2 has two negative signs (an even number), so it is positive: 40.
quiz.mistake: Counts the numbers instead of the negative signs

quiz.q: In a quiz, a correct answer gets +5 and a wrong answer gets −2. Kabir has 6 correct and 4 wrong answers. What is his score?
quiz.mistake: Adds the marks for wrong answers instead of taking them away

quiz.q: What is (−1) multiplied by itself 10 times?
quiz.explain: Each pair of (−1)s gives +1. Ten negative signs make five pairs, so the answer is 1.
steps: 10 negative signs is an even number
quiz.mistake: Thinks the answer is −10 or that the sign stays negative

quiz.explain: Each answer goes up by 4: −8, −4, 0, so next is 4. This shows negative × negative = positive.
steps: The answers go up by 4 each time
quiz.mistake: Thinks the answer must stay negative

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: how can (−3) × (−4) be +12? What are the sign rules for multiplying integers?
teach.praise: Wow! Same signs give plus, different signs give minus. Gappu's feathers are standing up in excitement!
teach.nudge: What sign do you get when both numbers are negative?

learn.hook: Division is multiplication played backwards — so the same sign rules work again!
points: Division undoes multiplication: (−20) ÷ 4 = −5 because 4 × (−5) = −20.
Same signs give a positive answer: (−20) ÷ (−4) = 5 and 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
Different signs give a negative answer: (−20) ÷ 4 = −5 and 20 ÷ (−4) = −5.
0 divided by any non-zero integer is 0.
Dividing by 0 is not defined — no number times 0 gives a non-zero number.

example.q: Find (−36) ÷ (−9) and check it.
steps: Both numbers are negative, so the answer is positive

learn.reallife: If a submarine goes down 60 m in 5 equal steps, each step is (−60) ÷ 5 = −12 m.

quiz.q: What is (−56) ÷ 8?
quiz.explain: Different signs give a negative answer. 56 ÷ 8 = 7, so the answer is −7.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the sign rule

quiz.explain: Same signs give a positive answer. 45 ÷ 9 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dividing two negatives gives a negative

quiz.q: What is 0 ÷ (−6)?
quiz.explain: 0 shared into any number of groups gives 0 in each. Check: (−6) × 0 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dividing by a negative must give a non-zero answer

quiz.q: What is 12 ÷ 0?
quiz.explain: No number multiplied by 0 gives 12, so 12 ÷ 0 has no answer. Division by zero is not defined.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything divided by 0 is 0

quiz.q: A diver goes down 60 m in 5 equal steps. What is the change in depth for each step?
quiz.explain: Going down is negative: (−60) ÷ 5 = −12 m each step.
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign for going down

quiz.q: Which has the same value as (−24) ÷ (−6)?
quiz.explain: (−24) ÷ (−6) = 4 (same signs give positive) and 24 ÷ 6 = 4 too.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the negative signs stay in the answer

quiz.q: The product of two integers is −72. One of them is 9. What is the other?
quiz.explain: The other integer = (−72) ÷ 9 = −8. Check: 9 × (−8) = −72.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the sign when dividing

quiz.q: The temperature fell from 10 degrees to −14 degrees in 6 hours, by the same amount each hour. What was the change each hour?
quiz.explain: Total change = −14 − 10 = −24 degrees. Each hour: (−24) ÷ 6 = −4 degrees.
quiz.mistake: Finds the total change but forgets to divide by the hours

teach.ask: Gappu must find (−36) ÷ (−9). How does he decide the sign of the answer when dividing integers?
teach.praise: Hooray! Same signs → positive, different signs → negative. (−36) ÷ (−9) = 4!
teach.nudge: What sign do you get when both numbers have the same sign?

learn.hook: Some rules let you swap, regroup and split numbers to make tough sums easy — like magic shortcuts!
points: Closure: adding, subtracting or multiplying two integers always gives an integer. Dividing may not: (−3) ÷ 2 is not an integer.
Commutative: a + b = b + a and a × b = b × a. This does NOT work for subtraction or division.
Associative: (a × b) × c = a × (b × c), and the same for addition. You can group in any way.
Distributive: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c. Example: (−8) × 102 = (−8) × 100 + (−8) × 2.
Identities: a + 0 = a and a × 1 = a. Also a × 0 = 0 and a × (−1) = −a.

example.q: Find (−25) × 37 × 4 the smart way.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers use the distributive property in their heads: 99 × ₹8 = 100 × ₹8 − ₹8 = ₹792.

games.title: Property check
items: Addition is commutative. Both sides are 2.
The left side is −11 and the right side is 11. Subtraction is not commutative.
Dividing one integer by another always gives an integer.
(−3) ÷ 2 = −1.5, which is not an integer.
Multiplying two integers always gives an integer.
Integers are closed under multiplication.
Any integer multiplied by 1 stays the same.
1 is the multiplicative identity.
Any integer times 0 is 0.

quiz.q: Which property does (−6) × 4 = 4 × (−6) show?
quiz.explain: The order of the two numbers is swapped and the product stays the same. That is the commutative property.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up commutative (swap) with associative (regroup)

quiz.q: Find (−25) × 37 × 4 using a smart grouping.
quiz.mistake: Loses a zero or the negative sign

quiz.q: Use the distributive property to find (−8) × 102.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies only the 100 part

quiz.q: a and b are integers and b is not 0. Which of these is NOT always an integer?
quiz.explain: a ÷ b can be a fraction, like 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5. The others always give integers.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all four operations are closed for integers

quiz.q: For integers, which operation is NOT commutative?
quiz.explain: 5 − 3 = 2 but 3 − 5 = −2, so the order matters for subtraction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every operation lets you swap the order

quiz.explain: Anything multiplied by 0 is 0, whatever the other numbers are.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies −15 by −7 and forgets the 0

quiz.q: Find 53 × (−7) + 47 × (−7) the smart way.
quiz.mistake: Loses the negative sign when combining

quiz.q: Which integer can multiply any integer and leave it unchanged?
quiz.explain: a × 1 = a for every integer a, so 1 is the multiplicative identity.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the identity for multiplication (1) with the one for addition (0)

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why (−4) × 7 and 7 × (−4) give the same answer. What is this property called and what does it say?
teach.praise: Brilliant! Swapping the order does not change a sum or a product. Gappu will use this shortcut forever!
teach.nudge: What happens to the answer when you swap the order of the numbers?

learn.hook: What is the biggest number that divides both 18 and 24 exactly? Let's hunt for it!
points: A factor of a number divides it exactly. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
A common factor divides two (or more) numbers exactly.
The HCF (Highest Common Factor) is the biggest common factor.
Prime factor method: write both numbers as products of primes and multiply the primes they share.
If the HCF of two numbers is 1, they are called co-prime, like 8 and 15.

example.q: Find the HCF of 18 and 24.

learn.reallife: Making the largest equal groups — like equal teams for a sports day or equal gift bags of sweets — uses the HCF.

quiz.q: What is the HCF of 18 and 24?
quiz.explain: The common factors of 18 and 24 are 1, 2, 3 and 6. The highest is 6.
quiz.mistake: Gives a common factor that is not the highest, or gives the LCM

quiz.q: Which list shows all the common factors of 20 and 30?
quiz.mistake: Lists multiples instead of factors, or includes a factor of only one number

quiz.q: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 and 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. What is the HCF of 36 and 60?
quiz.explain: The primes both share are 2, 2 and 3. HCF = 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Uses only one shared 2, or multiplies all the primes

quiz.q: Which pair of numbers is co-prime?
quiz.explain: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 15 = 3 × 5 share no prime, so their HCF is 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks co-prime numbers must both be prime

quiz.q: Meena has 24 red and 36 yellow flowers. She makes identical bunches using all the flowers. What is the greatest number of bunches she can make?
quiz.explain: The number of bunches must divide both 24 and 36. The biggest such number is HCF(24, 36) = 12. Each bunch has 2 red and 3 yellow.
quiz.mistake: Uses the LCM or the total instead of the HCF

quiz.q: What is the HCF of 17 and 34?
quiz.explain: 17 divides 34 exactly (34 = 2 × 17), so the biggest common factor is 17 itself.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a prime number always has HCF 1 with others

quiz.q: What is the HCF of any two different prime numbers?
quiz.explain: A prime has only 1 and itself as factors. Two different primes share only the factor 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the HCF is one of the primes

quiz.q: Two ribbons, 45 cm and 60 cm long, are cut into equal pieces that are as long as possible, with nothing left over. How long is each piece?
quiz.explain: The length must divide both 45 and 60. HCF(45, 60) = 15 cm. (3 pieces from the first, 4 from the second.)
quiz.mistake: Uses the LCM instead of the HCF

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know what the HCF of two numbers is. Explain it in your own words!
teach.praise: Ahaa! The biggest number that divides both — Gappu found the HCF of 18 and 24 is 6!
teach.nudge: Is the HCF the biggest or the smallest common factor?

learn.hook: Two friends skip-count — one by 6s, one by 8s. Which number will they both say first?
points: Multiples of a number are its times-table answers: multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, …
A common multiple is a multiple of both numbers.
The LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) is the smallest common multiple.
Prime factor method: take each prime the greatest number of times it appears in either number, and multiply.
For two numbers: HCF × LCM = the product of the numbers. For co-prime numbers the LCM is just their product.

example.q: Find the LCM of 6 and 8.
steps: The first one in both lists is 24

learn.reallife: Buying packs of 6 cups and packs of 8 plates so that the numbers match exactly needs the LCM.

items.text: The LCM of 4 and 6 is ___
The LCM of 5 and 7 is ___
The first common multiple of 3 and 4 is ___
8 and 12 have HCF 4, so their LCM is ___

quiz.q: What is the LCM of 6 and 8?
quiz.explain: The first number in both the 6 and 8 tables is 24.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the numbers (48) without checking for a smaller common multiple

quiz.q: Which list shows common multiples of 4 and 6?
quiz.explain: 12, 24 and 36 are in both the 4 table and the 6 table.
quiz.mistake: Picks multiples of only one of the numbers

quiz.q: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3. What is the LCM of 12 and 18?
quiz.explain: Take each prime the most times it appears: 2 twice (from 12) and 3 twice (from 18). LCM = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies all the primes from both numbers

quiz.q: What is the LCM of 7 and 9?
quiz.explain: 7 and 9 are co-prime (HCF 1), so their LCM is their product: 7 × 9 = 63.
quiz.mistake: Adds the numbers instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Two numbers have HCF 6 and LCM 72. One number is 18. What is the other number?
quiz.explain: HCF × LCM = product of the numbers. 6 × 72 = 432, and 432 ÷ 18 = 24.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the known number

quiz.q: What is the LCM of 5 and 20?
quiz.explain: 20 is already a multiple of 5, so the smallest common multiple is 20.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the two numbers out of habit

quiz.q: Can the LCM of two numbers be smaller than the bigger of the two numbers?
options: No, the LCM is at least as big as the bigger number
Yes, if the numbers are even
quiz.explain: The LCM must be a multiple of the bigger number, so it can never be smaller than it.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up LCM with HCF

quiz.q: For which pair is the LCM equal to the product of the two numbers?
quiz.explain: 4 and 9 are co-prime, so LCM = 4 × 9 = 36. For the others the LCM is smaller: 12, 18 and 30.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the LCM is always the product

teach.ask: Gappu skip-counts by 4s and his friend by 6s. What is the LCM, and how do they find it?
teach.praise: Yay! 12 is the first number both say. Gappu found the LCM!
teach.nudge: Is the LCM the smallest or the biggest common multiple?

topics.title: HCF and LCM in daily life

learn.hook: Two temple bells ring at different speeds. When will they ring together again? The LCM knows!
points: Use the HCF when you split things into the largest equal parts or the greatest number of equal groups.
Use the LCM when you want to know when things happen together again, or the smallest amount that fits several sizes.
The HCF is never bigger than the smaller number. The LCM is never smaller than the bigger number.
If one number divides the other, the HCF is the smaller number and the LCM is the bigger number.
Check your answer by dividing: the HCF must divide both numbers, and the LCM must be divisible by both numbers.

example.q: Two bells ring every 6 minutes and every 10 minutes. They ring together at 9:00 am. When will they next ring together?
steps: We need the LCM of 6 and 10

learn.reallife: Bus timetables, blinking festival lights and tiling a floor with the biggest square tiles all use HCF or LCM.

games.title: HCF or LCM?
items: Largest square tile that fits a floor exactly
When two buses next leave together
Greatest number of equal gift bags with nothing left over
Smallest number of laddoos that fill boxes of 6 or boxes of 8
Longest stick that measures 48 cm and 60 cm exactly
When two runners meet at the start line again

games.title: HCF and LCM truths
items: The HCF of two numbers is never bigger than the smaller number.
The HCF must divide the smaller number, so it cannot be bigger.
The LCM of 4 and 6 is 24.
24 is a common multiple, but 12 is the smallest one.
For two numbers, HCF × LCM = the product of the numbers.
Example: 4 and 6 have HCF 2 and LCM 12, and 2 × 12 = 24 = 4 × 6.
If one number divides the other, their HCF is the smaller number.
Example: HCF of 5 and 20 is 5.
Two even numbers can be co-prime.
Both have the factor 2, so their HCF is at least 2.
The LCM of two numbers is a multiple of their HCF.
The HCF divides both numbers, so it divides every common multiple too.

quiz.q: Two bells ring every 6 minutes and every 10 minutes. They ring together at 9:00 am. When will they next ring together?
quiz.explain: LCM of 6 and 10 is 30. So they ring together again 30 minutes later, at 9:30 am.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two times (16 minutes) or uses the HCF (2 minutes)

quiz.q: A floor is 12 m long and 18 m wide. What is the side of the largest square tile (in whole metres) that covers it exactly?
quiz.explain: The tile side must divide both 12 and 18. HCF(12, 18) = 6 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses the LCM instead of the HCF

quiz.q: What is the smallest number of laddoos that can be packed completely into boxes of 6, or completely into boxes of 8?
quiz.explain: The number must be a multiple of both 6 and 8. The smallest is LCM(6, 8) = 24.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 6 × 8 without looking for a smaller common multiple

quiz.q: Arjun runs one round of the track in 4 minutes and Kabir in 6 minutes. They start together. After how many minutes will both be at the start again?
quiz.explain: We need the LCM of 4 and 6, which is 12 minutes. Arjun has done 3 rounds and Kabir 2 rounds.
quiz.mistake: Adds the times or multiplies them

quiz.q: Two traffic lights change every 40 seconds and every 60 seconds. They change together now. After how many seconds will they next change together?
quiz.mistake: Uses the HCF (20) or adds the times

quiz.q: Joseph has 30 blue and 45 green marbles. He makes the greatest number of identical groups using all of them. How many green marbles are in each group?
quiz.explain: The greatest number of groups is HCF(30, 45) = 15. Each group gets 45 ÷ 15 = 3 green marbles (and 2 blue).
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of groups instead of the green marbles in each

quiz.q: What is the smallest number bigger than 1 that leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2, by 3 or by 4?
quiz.explain: LCM of 2, 3 and 4 is 12, which leaves remainder 0. Add 1: 13 leaves remainder 1 each time. (25 also works, but it is not the smallest.)
quiz.mistake: Gives the LCM and forgets to add the remainder

quiz.q: Diwali lights: red ones blink every 3 seconds, green every 5 seconds and blue every 6 seconds. They all blink together now. After how many seconds will they all blink together again?
quiz.explain: LCM of 3, 5 and 6: 3 and 6 give 6, and with 5 the LCM is 30 seconds.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies all three numbers (90) without finding the smallest common multiple

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: when should he use the HCF and when the LCM in a story problem?
teach.praise: Super! HCF for splitting into the biggest equal parts, LCM for meeting together again. Gappu is ready!
teach.nudge: Which one tells you when two things happen together again?

learn.hook: Can multiplying make a number SMALLER? With decimals like 0.5, it can — let's see how!
points: Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 moves the decimal point 1, 2 or 3 places to the right: 3.25 × 100 = 325.
Decimal × whole number: multiply as usual and keep the same number of decimal places: 1.2 × 3 = 3.6.
Decimal × decimal: multiply as whole numbers, then count the decimal places in both numbers and put that many in the answer.
Example: 2.4 × 0.3 → 24 × 3 = 72, with 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places → 0.72.
Multiplying by a decimal less than 1 gives a smaller answer: 8 × 0.5 = 4.

learn.hook: Arjun scored 32, 45, 18, 50 and 25 runs. Is he a '34-runs player'? The mean tells us his typical score!
points: Data is a collection of facts or numbers, like the runs scored in matches.
Putting data in a table makes it easier to read and compare.
The mean (average) = sum of all the values ÷ number of values.
The range = biggest value − smallest value. It shows how spread out the data is.
If every value goes up by the same amount, the mean goes up by that amount too.

example.q: Arjun's runs in 5 matches are 32, 45, 18, 50 and 25. Find the mean and the range.

learn.reallife: Cricket batting averages, average marks in a class and the average rainfall of a month are all means.

games.title: Mean truths
items: The mean is always one of the numbers in the data.
The mean of 1 and 2 is 1.5, which is not in the data.
Mean = sum of the values ÷ number of values.
That is how the mean is found.
If every value is increased by 2, the mean also increases by 2.
The sum grows by 2 for each value, so the mean grows by 2.
The range is the biggest value minus the smallest value.
It measures the spread of the data.
The mean of 0, 0, 0 and 12 is 12.
Sum 12 ÷ 4 values = 3.
Adding a new value equal to the mean does not change the mean.
Example: 2, 4, 6 has mean 4; 2, 4, 6, 4 also has mean 4.

learn.hook: If one billionaire walks into a tea stall, the 'average' wealth there shoots up! The median stays calm. Let's see why.
points: The median is the middle value after arranging the data from smallest to largest.
If there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
The mode is the value that appears most often. Data can have more than one mode.
One very big or very small value can pull the mean far away, but the median hardly changes.
Use the mode for 'most popular' questions, like the most common shoe size.

steps: 7 values, so the middle one is the 4th: 6

learn.hook: Can you find the exact middle of a line without measuring? A compass can do it — like a magic trick!
points: To bisect means to cut into two equal parts.
Perpendicular bisector of AB: with a compass opening MORE than half of AB, draw arcs from A and from B on both sides. Join the two points where the arcs cross.
The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint of AB and makes a 90° angle with it.
Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is the same distance from A and from B.
Angle bisector: from the vertex draw an arc cutting both arms. From those two points draw arcs that cross. Join the vertex to the crossing point. It splits the angle into two equal halves.

example.q: Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB = 6 cm. Where does it cut AB?
steps: Open the compass to more than 3 cm (say 4 cm)
Draw arcs above and below AB from A, then from B with the same opening
Join the two crossing points; it cuts AB at its midpoint M
example.answer: At M, where AM = MB = 3 cm, at a right angle

learn.reallife: Builders find the middle of a wall, and gardeners mark paths that stay equally far from two trees, using the perpendicular bisector idea.

games.title: Perpendicular bisector steps

games.title: Bisector truths
items: The perpendicular bisector of AB meets AB at 90°.
That is why it is called perpendicular.
Every point on the perpendicular bisector of AB is equally far from A and B.
This is the special property of the perpendicular bisector.
For a perpendicular bisector, the compass opening can be less than half of AB.
Then the arcs from A and B would not meet.
An angle bisector splits an angle into two equal angles.
Bisect means cut into two equal parts.
Bisecting a 90° angle gives two 30° angles.
Half of 90° is 45°.
We need a protractor to draw a perpendicular bisector.
A ruler and a compass are enough.

quiz.q: AB = 8 cm. Its perpendicular bisector cuts AB at M. How long is AM?
quiz.explain: The perpendicular bisector cuts AB at its midpoint, so AM = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the bisector meets AB at the middle

quiz.q: What angle does the perpendicular bisector of AB make with AB?
quiz.explain: Perpendicular means it meets AB at a right angle, 90°.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'bisector' (half) with the angle it makes

quiz.q: To draw the perpendicular bisector of a 6 cm segment, what compass opening should you use?
quiz.explain: The opening must be more than half of 6 cm (3 cm), otherwise the arcs from the two ends will not meet.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any small opening works

quiz.q: An angle of 80° is bisected. What is each new angle?
quiz.explain: Bisecting cuts the angle into two equal parts: 80° ÷ 2 = 40°.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle instead of halving it

quiz.q: P is a point on the perpendicular bisector of AB, and PA = 5 cm. What is PB?
quiz.explain: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from A and B, so PB = PA = 5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Halves or doubles the distance

quiz.q: A 60° angle is bisected, and then one of the halves is bisected again. What is the smallest angle made?
quiz.mistake: Bisects only once

quiz.explain: The compass draws the arcs and the ruler joins the crossing points.
quiz.mistake: Thinks angles must be measured with a protractor

quiz.q: In an angle bisector construction, why are the two new angles equal?
options: The two triangles formed are congruent by SSS, so the matching angles are equal
quiz.explain: The arcs make two triangles with all three sides equal (SSS). Congruent triangles have equal matching angles.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the construction to congruent triangles

learn.hook: No protractor? No problem! With only a compass you can make 60°, 30°, 90°, 45° and even 120°.
points: 60°: draw an arc from the vertex, then an arc of the SAME radius from where it cuts the arm. The three points form an equilateral triangle, so the angle is 60°.
120°: step the same arc twice along the first arc (60° + 60°).
30° = bisect 60°. 90° = construct a perpendicular. 45° = bisect 90°.
Square: all four sides equal and all angles 90°. Rectangle: opposite sides equal and all angles 90°.
Circle: open the compass to the radius, keep the point fixed and turn.

example.q: Construct an angle of 30° using only a ruler and a compass.
steps: Construct a 60° angle using arcs of the same radius

learn.reallife: Carpenters, tailors and rangoli artists use these exact angles to make neat, matching patterns.

quiz.q: How can you construct a 30° angle with a ruler and a compass?
quiz.explain: 60° ÷ 2 = 30°, so bisecting a constructed 60° angle gives 30°.
quiz.mistake: Bisects the wrong angle (90° ÷ 2 = 45°)

quiz.q: What angle do you get by bisecting a right angle?
quiz.explain: A right angle is 90°. Half of it is 45°.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the 60° construction with the 90° one

quiz.q: In the 60° construction, why is the angle exactly 60°?

quiz.explain: All three distances are the same compass radius, so the triangle is equilateral and each angle is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the hidden equilateral triangle

learn.hook: Why are bathroom tiles squares and beehive cells hexagons — but never pentagons? Let's crack the tiling code!
points: A tiling covers a flat surface with shapes that leave no gaps and do not overlap.
At every point where corners meet, the angles must add up to 360°.
Only three regular polygons tile on their own: equilateral triangles (6 × 60°), squares (4 × 90°) and regular hexagons (3 × 120°).
A regular pentagon has 108° angles. 360 ÷ 108 is not a whole number, so pentagons leave gaps.
Different shapes can tile together: two regular octagons (135° each) and one square (90°) fit around a point.

example.q: Can regular pentagons tile a floor on their own?
steps: Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°
No whole number of pentagons makes exactly 360°

learn.reallife: Floor tiles, brick walls, honeycombs and rangoli borders are all tilings. Some old Indian palaces have amazing tiled floors and windows!

A tiling has no gaps and no overlaps.
The angles meeting at a point in a tiling add up to 360°.
They go all the way around the point.
Regular hexagons can tile a floor.
Regular pentagons can tile a floor on their own.
108° does not fit into 360° a whole number of times.
Six equilateral triangles fit around one point.
Circles can tile a floor without gaps.
Circles always leave curved gaps between them.

quiz.q: In a floor of square tiles, how many squares meet at each corner point?
quiz.explain: Each square corner is 90°. 360° ÷ 90° = 4 squares.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the angles must make a full 360°

quiz.q: How many equilateral triangles meet at a point in a triangle tiling?
quiz.explain: Each angle is 60°. 360° ÷ 60° = 6 triangles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 3 triangles meet because a triangle has 3 corners

quiz.q: Each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°. How many hexagons meet at a point in a honeycomb tiling?
quiz.explain: 360° ÷ 120° = 3 hexagons.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 6 meet because a hexagon has 6 sides

quiz.q: Why can't regular pentagons tile a floor on their own?
options: Their 108° angles do not fit into 360° a whole number of times
Pentagons have an odd number of sides
quiz.explain: 3 pentagons make 324° (gap) and 4 make 432° (overlap). No whole number gives exactly 360°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks having an odd number of sides is the reason

quiz.q: Regular octagons (135° each) and squares tile together. At each point, 2 octagons meet. How many squares are needed there?
quiz.explain: 2 × 135° = 270°. 360° − 270° = 90°, which is exactly one square corner.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the octagon angles from 360°

quiz.q: At a point in a tiling, the angles are 90°, 60°, 60° and x. What is x?
quiz.explain: All angles around the point add up to 360°. x = 360° − 90° − 60° − 60° = 150°.
quiz.mistake: Uses 180° instead of 360°

quiz.q: Which shape can NOT tile a floor on its own?
quiz.explain: A regular octagon has 135° angles. 2 × 135° = 270° and 3 × 135° = 405°, so octagons alone leave gaps.
quiz.mistake: Thinks shapes with more sides fit together better

quiz.q: Meena's room floor is 3 m by 2 m. She uses square tiles of side 50 cm. How many tiles does she need?
quiz.explain: Along 3 m: 300 ÷ 50 = 6 tiles. Along 2 m: 200 ÷ 50 = 4 tiles. Total = 6 × 4 = 24 tiles.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change metres into centimetres

teach.ask: Gappu wants to tile his nest floor. What rules must the tiles follow, and why do hexagons work?
teach.praise: Ahaa! No gaps, no overlaps, and the corners make 360°. Gappu's nest looks like a honeycomb now!
teach.nudge: What must the angles at a meeting point add up to?

learn.hook: An equation is like a riddle with an equals sign in the middle. Can you find the secret number that makes it true?
points: An equation says that two expressions are equal, like x + 7 = 15. It always has an = sign.
The letter stands for an unknown number.
The value of the letter that makes the equation true is called its solution.
Check a solution by putting it in place of the letter: if both sides match, it is correct.
Word stories can be turned into equations: 'a number plus 7 is 15' becomes x + 7 = 15.

example.q: Riya thinks of a number, adds 7 and gets 15. Write an equation and find the number.
steps: Which number plus 7 makes 15? x = 8. Check: 8 + 7 = 15 ✓

learn.reallife: When a shopkeeper says '3 pens and a ₹10 eraser cost ₹40', there is a hidden equation for the price of one pen.

games.title: Equation or not?
items: x = 4 is the solution of x + 6 = 10.
4 + 6 = 10, so both sides match.
The solution of 5x = 20 is x = 15.
5 × 15 = 75. The solution is x = 4, because 5 × 4 = 20.
2x + 3 is an equation.
It has no = sign. It is an expression.
y = 3 makes 4y − 2 = 10 true.
An equation must always have an = sign.
The = sign shows that the two sides are equal.
3 + 4 = 7 has an unknown number in it.
It has no letter, so there is nothing unknown to find.

quiz.q: Which of these is an equation?
quiz.explain: Only 4x − 1 = 11 has an = sign joining two sides.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any expression with a letter is an equation

quiz.q: Is x = 3 the solution of 2x + 5 = 11?
quiz.explain: Put x = 3: 2 × 3 + 5 = 6 + 5 = 11. Both sides are 11, so x = 3 is the solution.
quiz.mistake: Makes an arithmetic slip while checking

quiz.q: Arjun is a years old. In 5 years he will be 17. Which equation fits?
quiz.explain: In 5 years his age will be a + 5, and that equals 17.
quiz.mistake: Turns 'in 5 years' into a subtraction

quiz.q: Solve x + 9 = 20.
quiz.explain: Which number plus 9 makes 20? 20 − 9 = 11. Check: 11 + 9 = 20.
quiz.mistake: Adds 9 to 20 instead of subtracting

quiz.q: 6 pens cost ₹90. If one pen costs p rupees, then 6p = 90. What is p?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 90 by 6 instead of dividing

quiz.q: Which value of y makes 3y − 4 = 14 true?
quiz.mistake: Stops after adding 4 to 14 and forgets to divide by 3

quiz.q: Meena cut a ribbon of length L cm into 4 equal pieces of 15 cm each. So L ÷ 4 = 15. What is L?
quiz.mistake: Divides 15 by 4 instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Kabir thinks of a number n, multiplies it by 3, then subtracts 5 and gets 16. Which equation shows this?
quiz.explain: First multiply by 3 (3n), then subtract 5 (3n − 5). The result is 16.
quiz.mistake: Puts the steps in the wrong order

teach.ask: Gappu heard the word 'equation'. What is an equation, and what does 'solution' mean?
teach.praise: Tweet! Both sides are equal, and the solution makes it true. Gappu wants more riddles!
teach.nudge: What sign does every equation have, and what does the solution do?

learn.hook: An equation is like a see-saw in perfect balance. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other — and it stays balanced!
points: Think of an equation as a balance: both sides weigh the same.
You may add, subtract, multiply or divide BOTH sides by the same number (not dividing by 0). The balance stays.
Use the opposite operation to undo: undo + 4 by subtracting 4; undo × 3 by dividing by 3.
For two-step equations, undo the adding or subtracting first, then the multiplying or dividing.
Always check by putting the answer back into the original equation.

example.q: Solve 3x + 4 = 19.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers balancing a scale with weights on one side and rice on the other are solving an equation!

games.title: Steps to solve 2x + 7 = 19
items: Start: 2x + 7 = 19
Subtract 7 from both sides: 2x = 12
Divide both sides by 2: x = 6

quiz.q: Solve x − 7 = 12.
quiz.explain: Add 7 to both sides: x = 12 + 7 = 19. Check: 19 − 7 = 12.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 7 again instead of adding

quiz.q: Solve 5y = 35.
quiz.explain: Divide both sides by 5: y = 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 5 instead of dividing by 5

quiz.q: Solve 3x + 4 = 19.
quiz.explain: Subtract 4: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5. Check: 3 × 5 + 4 = 19.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 3x = 15 and gives 15 as the answer

quiz.q: What is the best first step to solve 4x − 3 = 21?
quiz.explain: Undo the − 3 first by adding 3 to both sides: 4x = 24. Then divide by 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses the same operation instead of the opposite one

quiz.q: Solve a ÷ 4 + 2 = 6.
quiz.explain: Subtract 2: a ÷ 4 = 4. Multiply by 4: a = 16. Check: 16 ÷ 4 + 2 = 6.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 6 by 4 before subtracting 2

quiz.q: Solve 2(x + 3) = 18.
quiz.explain: Divide both sides by 2: x + 3 = 9. Subtract 3: x = 6. Check: 2 × (6 + 3) = 18.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 3 from 18 before dividing by 2

quiz.q: Solve 7 = 2y − 5.
quiz.explain: Add 5 to both sides: 12 = 2y. Divide by 2: y = 6. Check: 2 × 6 − 5 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 5 instead of adding

quiz.q: Riya says the solution of 3x + 6 = 21 is x = 9. What is the correct solution?
quiz.explain: Check x = 9: 3 × 9 + 6 = 33, not 21. Correct: 3x = 21 − 6 = 15, so x = 5.
quiz.mistake: Does not check the answer by putting it back

teach.ask: Gappu wants to solve 2x + 7 = 19 by balancing. What steps should he follow?
teach.praise: Fantastic! Subtract 7, divide by 2, and check: x = 6. Gappu's see-saw is balanced!
teach.nudge: Whatever you do to one side of the equation, what must you do to the other?

learn.hook: Every story problem hides an equation. Find it, solve it, and the mystery number pops out!
points: Read the story carefully and decide what the unknown is. Give it a letter.
Write the other amounts using that letter, like 'the next number' = n + 1 or 'three times as old' = 3x.
Make an equation from the fact the story gives (the total, the perimeter, the sum of angles…).
Solve the equation by balancing.
Check the answer in the story, not just in the equation.

example.q: The sum of two consecutive numbers is 41. Find the numbers.
steps: Let the smaller number be n; the next one is n + 1
2n = 40, so n = 20; the numbers are 20 and 21 (check: 20 + 21 = 41)

learn.reallife: Finding someone's age from a clue, the cost of one item from a bill, or a missing angle all use equations.

items.text: If n is a number, the next number is ___
A square of side s has perimeter 36 cm, so ___ = 36
Kabir is x years old and his father is 3 times as old. Father's age = ___
If 2x = 24, then x = ___

games.title: Equation or expression?
items: 4m
n + n + n

quiz.q: The sum of two consecutive numbers is 41. What is the smaller number?
quiz.explain: n + (n + 1) = 41, so 2n + 1 = 41, 2n = 40 and n = 20. The numbers are 20 and 21.
quiz.mistake: Gives the bigger number, or halves 41 without thinking

quiz.q: A father is 3 times as old as his son Kabir. Their ages add up to 48 years. How old is Kabir?
quiz.explain: Let Kabir be x. Father = 3x. x + 3x = 4x = 48, so x = 12. Father is 36. Check: 12 + 36 = 48.
quiz.mistake: Divides 48 by 3 instead of by 4

quiz.q: A rectangle's length is 3 cm more than its breadth. Its perimeter is 26 cm. What is the breadth?
quiz.explain: Breadth b, length b + 3. Perimeter 2(b + b + 3) = 26, so 2b + 3 = 13, 2b = 10, b = 5 cm. Length is 8 cm. Check: 2 × (5 + 8) = 26.
quiz.mistake: Gives the length instead of the breadth

quiz.q: A triangle has angles x, x and 80°. What is x?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2

quiz.q: Aisha has ₹50 more than Harpreet. Together they have ₹230. How much does Harpreet have?
quiz.explain: Harpreet h, Aisha h + 50. h + h + 50 = 230, so 2h = 180 and h = ₹90. Aisha has ₹140. Check: 90 + 140 = 230.
quiz.mistake: Halves 230 without taking away the extra ₹50

quiz.q: Train tickets cost ₹35 each. A group pays ₹420 in all. How many tickets did they buy?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts or adds instead of dividing

quiz.q: I think of a number, multiply it by 4, add 10 and get 50. What is my number?
quiz.mistake: Divides 50 by 4 without first taking away 10

quiz.q: Joseph buys 3 notebooks and a pen that costs ₹5. He pays ₹95 in all. What does one notebook cost?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 3 after subtracting the pen

teach.ask: Gappu has a story: 'Twice a number plus 3 is 15.' How does he solve a word problem like this using an equation?
teach.praise: Brilliant! 2n + 3 = 15, so n = 6. Gappu solved his first story problem!
teach.nudge: What should he call the unknown number, and what does he write next?
